clue.text: With respect to area around Norfolk, Everyman has to be obnoxious

blocks.note: 'of' can mean concerning or with respect to
the Fens are the flat marshy region of eastern England bordering Norfolk
the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I
'has' as in 'I have' contracts to 've

explanation.surface: A complaint that the setter has become unbearable over something to do with East Anglia.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are low-lying farmland in eastern England, next to Norfolk; setters often call themselves I, and 'has' shrinks to 've.
explanation.definitionFit: Something offensive is objectionable and unpleasant, a close synonym of obnoxious behaviour or remarks.

clue.text: Serf working across terrain in mediaeval principality

indicators.note: letters that are working are set in motion and rearranged
one word lies across another, spanning it on both sides so it sits inside

blocks.note: the letters of serf rearranged
terrain is ground or land

explanation.surface: A medieval peasant toiling on the fields of some feudal principality.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged serf letters split around the terrain word, one letter before and three after.
explanation.definitionFit: Flanders was a powerful county in the Low Countries during the Middle Ages, a historic territory ruled by counts.

clue.text: Losing head, stop being calm

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

blocks.note: to stop is to cease

explanation.surface: Advice to someone panicking: drop the leadership role and stop trying to stay composed.
explanation.walkthrough: CEASE without its first letter C leaves EASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease pain or worry is to soothe or relieve it, so the verb works as a synonym.

clue.text: ‘Clue is “Fish”.’ ‘Flounders.’ ‘That’s how it goes’

indicators.note: to flounder is to struggle clumsily, so the quoted letters tumble into disorder

blocks.note: the quoted clue's words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A crossword exchange: one person gives the clue 'Fish', the other answers 'Flounders', and a shrug follows.
explanation.walkthrough: Flounders looks like the answer to 'Fish', since a flounder is a flatfish, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Such is life is a resigned idiom accepting that misfortune happens, exactly the shrugging sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Italian scorer, clever dick to some extent

indicators.note: only to some extent means only part of the phrase is used, a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: found running across the end of clever and start of dick

explanation.surface: A smart-aleck Italian goal-scorer, a little too clever for his own good.
explanation.walkthrough: Scorer suggests football, but here it is someone who writes musical scores.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian composer of operas such as Aida, and a composer writes scores.

clue.text: Now – regrettably – Dad’s eating hay

indicators.note: something that has gone regrettably has gone wrong, so the letters are put out of order

blocks.note: every letter of the phrase used

explanation.surface: Someone lamenting that father has, sadly, taken to eating hay these days.
explanation.walkthrough: Eating looks like a container signal putting one word inside another, but it is simply part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for the present era, meaning at the current time or nowadays.

clue.text: Biscuit mix

blocks.note: first meaning: a popular British oat biscuit sold under that brand name
second meaning: to socialise or rub shoulders with others

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like baking instructions; HOBNOB is a crunchy British oat biscuit and also a verb for mingling.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobnob names a well-known oaty cookie brand, and as a verb means mingle socially with important people.

clue.text: Exercise and hot drink proposed by Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so whatever he proposes has its initial sounds exchanged

blocks.note: a spiced Indian tea drink, served hot

explanation.surface: A wellness routine: a workout followed by a warm cup of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of CHAI TEA and you get TAI CHI.
explanation.definitionFit: Tai chi is a Chinese martial art practised as slow, flowing movements for health, a form of physical workout.

clue.text: Revising hastily at last? There’s nothing more to add

indicators.note: revising means reworking and changing, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: every letter of the three words

explanation.surface: A student cramming for an exam at the last moment, deciding nothing else needs saying.
explanation.walkthrough: At last looks like a signal to take a final letter, but both words belong to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said when something sums a situation up completely, leaving no need for further comment.

clue.text: Laugh abruptly with derisive interjections following excitement

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun; the definition is singular

indicators.note: cut off abruptly means the word stops short, losing its final letter

blocks.note: a hoot is a loud laugh
mocking cries of 'hah!'

explanation.surface: Someone who scoffs and laughs sharply after all the fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: HOOT cut short to HOO, then HAHS.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-hah is a commotion or fuss, so hoo-hahs are bouts of agitated, noisy commotion.

clue.text: A Rover’s waxed, for starters, when money’s seen around here!

definitions.text: A Rover’s waxed, for starters, when money’s seen around here!

indicators.note: starters are the opening letters of each of the preceding words
one thing seen around another surrounds it, holding it inside

blocks.note: the opening letters of the three words
cash is money

explanation.surface: A Rover car gets a polish once payment is handed over at the valeting place.
explanation.walkthrough: Rover is a British car make, and the whole clue also describes the place: you pay and your car gets waxed.
explanation.definitionFit: A car wash is a facility where vehicles are cleaned and polished for a fee, which the whole sentence pictures.

clue.text: Where you find some heresy? No; dogma!

definitions.text: Where you find some heresy? No; dogma!

indicators.note: some of the following words means just a part of them, a consecutive run of letters

blocks.note: spans the end of heresy, all of no and the start of dogma

explanation.surface: A churchgoer insisting that a church council deals in orthodox teaching, not heresy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: a synod is where church doctrine is laid down, not heresy.
explanation.definitionFit: A synod is an assembly of clergy that rules on church doctrine, so it is a place where official teaching is set.

clue.text: Nine getting into pastry, sliced for a do

indicators.note: something getting into another goes inside it

blocks.note: a pie is a pastry dish
Roman numeral for nine
sliced means cut

explanation.surface: Pastry slices being prepared for a party of nine guests.
explanation.walkthrough: Do looks like a party, but here it is short for hairdo.
explanation.definitionFit: A pixie cut is a very short cropped hairstyle, and a do is informal shorthand for a hairdo.

clue.text: One who told tales when cradle rocked

indicators.note: rocked means shaken about, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: both words, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A sneak who told on others back when still a baby in the cradle.
explanation.walkthrough: Told tales suggests a telltale, but here it means wrote stories.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence was an English novelist and short-story writer, so a teller of tales in the literary sense.

clue.text: Concert venue, a large place in which to fall asleep entirely

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

blocks.clueFragment: place in which to fall asleep
blocks.note: a berth is a bunk on a ship or train
all means wholly or entirely

explanation.surface: A complaint that a concert hall is so roomy and dull you could doze off completely.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Albert Hall is a famous London concert hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Albert Hall in London hosts the Proms and many concerts, making it a famous music venue.

clue.text: A young woman almost flipped somewhere in Latvia

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the word loses its last letter
something flipped is turned over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
a girl is a young woman

explanation.surface: A young woman nearly loses it somewhere on a trip to the Baltic.
explanation.walkthrough: A GIRL loses its L, then A GIR is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Riga is the capital city of Latvia, so it is indeed a place within that Baltic country.

clue.text: A minion’s faltering complaint

indicators.note: faltering means unsteady and stumbling, so the letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: all the letters of both words

explanation.surface: An underling stammering out a grievance to the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: Complaint looks like a grumble, but here it means an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Insomnia is a medical disorder of being unable to sleep, and complaint can mean an illness or ailment.

clue.text: They made ‘SOS’ a palindrome

blocks.note: surface reading: someone turned the distress signal into a word that reads the same both ways
setter's reading: the Swedish pop group who recorded the hit song SOS, and whose own name reads the same backwards

explanation.walkthrough: SOS is itself a palindrome, which makes the clue look like wordplay about the letters; really it points to the band behind the 1975 song and their palindromic name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish quartet recorded the single SOS, and their four-letter band name reads identically in either direction.

clue.text: Supports British experts

blocks.note: BR is a standard abbreviation for British
aces are people highly skilled at something

explanation.surface: British specialists are backing some cause.
explanation.walkthrough: Braces are also what Americans call suspenders, the straps holding up trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Braces are structural props or straps that hold something up, so they act as supports.

clue.text: Gaffer isn’t swayed by facetious excuse for typo in text

definitions.text: facetious excuse for typo in text

indicators.note: swayed means moved to and fro, so the letters are shifted into a fresh order

blocks.note: all letters of both words

explanation.surface: A football manager unmoved by a player's jokey explanation for a misspelled message.
explanation.walkthrough: A gaffer is British slang for a boss or football manager.
explanation.definitionFit: Blaming fat fingers is a jokey way of excusing mistyped keys on a phone or keyboard.

clue.text: What’s displayed by keener gymnasts, in part?

definitions.text: What’s displayed by keener gymnasts, in part?

indicators.note: in part means only a portion of the words is used, a consecutive run of letters

blocks.note: spans the end of keener and the start of gymnasts

explanation.surface: A question about what the more enthusiastic gymnasts are showing.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also defines: eager gymnasts show vigour.
explanation.definitionFit: Energy is vigour and liveliness, exactly what keen athletes show when they perform.

clue.text: Release redacted; it’s inevitable

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase; the definition is a clause

indicators.note: releasing letters sets them free to fall in a new arrangement

blocks.note: all its letters

explanation.surface: Someone resigned that a blacked-out document will eventually be published.
explanation.walkthrough: A dead cert, British slang from horse racing, is something certain to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead cert is an absolute certainty, something bound to happen, which is what calling an outcome inevitable says.

clue.text: What cowboys may carry; what may carry cowboys

blocks.note: first meaning: revolvers made by the Colt company
second meaning: young male horses

explanation.walkthrough: The mirrored phrasing invites one meaning twice; the gun brand and the young horse are separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Colt revolvers are classic Wild West sidearms, and colts are young stallions that riders may mount.

clue.text: Hush-hush, not about to become public

indicators.note: not about means the abbreviation for about, c or circa, is taken away

blocks.note: covert means secret

explanation.surface: A secret that stops being secret and goes public.
explanation.walkthrough: C is short for circa, about; COVERT minus C leaves OVERT.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means openly shown rather than hidden, the opposite of secret, so done in public view.

clue.text: Primarily, announcement showing incredulity flatly!

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letters of the words are taken

blocks.note: the opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Someone declaring disbelief in a deadpan voice.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: 'As if!' is a flat exclamation of disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: As if is a slangy retort meaning that is not going to happen, a curt way of saying you doubt something.

clue.text: Carelessly malinger without a reason for machine's downtime

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter a is taken out
done carelessly means done sloppily, so the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: all its letters

explanation.surface: A worker carelessly skiving with no excuse, leaving the machines idle.
explanation.walkthrough: MALINGER loses its A, and the remaining letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A gremlin is an imaginary mischievous creature blamed for unexplained mechanical faults and breakdowns.

clue.text: Anglesey spending year struggling to become member of African Union

indicators.note: spending something means giving it up, so a letter is lost
struggling suggests thrashing about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: all its letters
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A Welsh island, losing a year in its struggles, applying to join an African bloc.
explanation.walkthrough: Anglesey is an island off north-west Wales; remove Y and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Senegal is a West African nation and one of the member states of the continental African Union.

clue.text: Where Douglas is breaking flamingoes – not good

indicators.note: not good means the abbreviation g for good is removed
something breaking falls to pieces, so the letters reassemble differently

blocks.note: all its letters
G is short for good

explanation.surface: A man named Douglas badly scattering a flock of flamingos.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas looks like a person, but it is the capital of the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas is the capital town of the Isle of Man, so the island is the place where it sits.
